title: Completed etale groupoid at a finite stabilizer
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field, let $\mathcal X$ be a finite-type Deligne--Mumford stack over $k$ with finite diagonal, and let $x\in\mathcal X(k)$. Use the stack and Deligne--Mumford conventions of [def-sfb-stable-pointed-moduli-groupoids]. There is an etale scheme atlas $p:T\to\mathcal X$ with a point $u\in T(k)$ and an identification $p(u)\simeq x$. Write $R=T\times_{\mathcal X}T$, with source $s$, target $t$, identity and composition, and $H=\operatorname{Aut}(x)$. The fibre of $R\to T\times_kT$ at $(u,u)$ is a finite reduced set indexed by $H$. Put $A=\widehat{\mathcal O}_{T,u}$, the maximal-ideal-adic completion [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion]. The completion of $R$ along that finite set is the disjoint union of the completions $\widehat R_h$ at its points, and both $s:\widehat R_h\to\operatorname{Spf}A$ and $t:\widehat R_h\to\operatorname{Spf}A$ are isomorphisms for each $h\in H$. Identity and composition reduce to the identity and composition in $H$. The stackification of this completed groupoid presents the formal completion of $\mathcal X$ along the residual gerbe of $x$, meaning the substack of objects locally isomorphic to $x$. Here formal schemes mean the systems of their nilpotent thickenings. The object over $\operatorname{Spf}A$ is induced by the effective morphism $\operatorname{Spec}A\to T\to\mathcal X$, and every completed arrow supplies a compatible isomorphism of the two pulled-back objects on every thickening. Schemes and etaleness are [def-pc-scheme] and [def-weil-etale-morphism].

source.place: Tag 0DR3, Remark remark-groupoid-defo (completed groupoid presentation); etale.tex Tag 039M, Lemma lemma-characterize-etale-completions (completed source and target maps). The finite-stabilizer decomposition is the finite-diagonal etale specialization.

proof.text: Use the finite-type atlas convention to choose a surjective etale scheme atlas $T\to\mathcal X$ with $T$ of finite type over $k$. The base change $E=\operatorname{Spec}k\times_{x,\mathcal X}T$ is a scheme by the finite-diagonal convention, and $E\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is etale and surjective by the atlas definition. Its nonempty fibre is a disjoint union of spectra of finite separable extensions of $k$. Each extension is $k$, since $k$ is algebraically closed. Choose one component. Its map to $T$ gives $u\in T(k)$ and its 2-fibre-product datum gives the specified identification $p(u)\simeq x$.

The finite-diagonal convention represents $R=T\times_{\mathcal X}T$ by a scheme finite over $T\times_kT$. Its projections $s,t:R\to T$ are etale, being the two base changes of the atlas. The scheme $D=R\times_{T\times_kT}\operatorname{Spec}k$ at $(u,u)$ represents $\operatorname{Isom}(p(u),p(u))$: the two maps to $T$ are fixed, so the remaining datum is precisely that isomorphism. By the DM Isom-space lemma this scheme is unramified over $k$. It is affine, being finite over $k$. The unramified-algebra lemma therefore writes its ring as a finite product of finite separable extensions of $k$, all equal to $k$. Thus $D=\coprod_{h\in H}\operatorname{Spec}k$, with indexing supplied by conjugation with $p(u)\simeq x$. This also proves finiteness of $H$, rather than assuming it.

proof.text: The scheme $T$ is Noetherian by finite type over the Noetherian scheme $\operatorname{Spec}k$ (a field has only the ideals $0,k$). In particular $T$ is locally Noetherian, so by that definition $u$ lies in an affine open $V=\operatorname{Spec}C\subseteq T$ with $C$ a Noetherian ring; $\mathcal O_{T,u}$ is the localization of $C$ at the prime of $u$, hence Noetherian by localization permanence. The etale maps $s,t:R\to T$ are unramified, hence locally of finite type: the preimage of every affine open of $T$, in particular $s^{-1}(V)$, is covered by spectra of finitely generated algebras over its ring. Each $r_h$ maps to $u$ under $s$, so it has an affine open neighbourhood $\operatorname{Spec}C_h\subseteq s^{-1}(V)$ with $C_h$ a finitely generated $C$-algebra. Then $C_h$ is Noetherian by finite-type algebra permanence, and its local ring at $r_h$ is Noetherian by localization permanence. Put $B=\mathcal O_{T,u}$, $A=\widehat B$, and $B_h=\mathcal O_{R,r_h}$. Their maximal ideals are finitely generated. The completion-mod-power lemma identifies every quotient of $A$ by $(\mathfrak m_B A)^N$ with $B/\mathfrak m_B^N$, and similarly for $\widehat B_h$. Completion is therefore exactly the compatible system of these pointed nilpotent neighbourhoods. The local-completion lemma identifies the maximal ideal of $A$ with $\mathfrak m_B A$.

proof.text: Apply the etale completed-local-ring lemma to $s:R\to T$ at each $r_h$: its closed-point conclusion shows that $u$ and $r_h$ are closed. Thus $(u,u)$ is a closed $k$-point of $T\times_kT$, and its fibre $D\subset R$ is a closed finite reduced subscheme. Write $\mathcal I_D$ for its ideal. Every neighbourhood cut out by $\mathcal I_D^N$ has underlying space $|D|$, a finite discrete space. Its singleton open-and-closed pieces are disjoint and exhaust it. The ring on the piece at $r_h$ is its stalk, namely $B_h/(\mathcal I_D B_h)^N$. Since $D$ is reduced with residue field $k$ at $r_h$, $\mathcal I_D B_h$ is the maximal ideal of $B_h$. These identifications commute with reduction in $N$. Taking the systems gives $\widehat R_D=\coprod_h\operatorname{Spf}\widehat B_h$. This is a decomposition of infinitesimal neighbourhoods, not a claim that the points admit disjoint open neighbourhoods in $R$.

proof.text: Apply the etale completed-local-ring lemma to $s:R\to T$ and to $t:R\to T$, at each $r_h$ above $u$. The target is locally finite type over the algebraically closed field $k$, both maps are etale, and both points are $k$-rational by steps 1--2. The induced maps $A\to\widehat B_h$ are isomorphisms. Hence both maps $\widehat R_h\to\operatorname{Spf}A$ are isomorphisms of formal schemes. They preserve maximal ideals and every power, so this assertion holds on every specified thickening, compatibly with its reduction maps.

proof.text: Restrict identity, inverse and composition of the 2-fibre-product groupoid to the completed systems. Under the source isomorphism of step 5, write the component indexed by $h$ as the unique arrow $a_h(z)$ with source $z$, and put $\alpha_h=t\circ s_h^{-1}$. Each $\alpha_h$ is an automorphism preserving the maximal ideal and all its powers. The composable pair $a_g(z),a_h(\alpha_g(z))$ has composite reducing to $r_{hg}$, where $hg=h\circ g$ in $H$, and source $z$. Composition induces a map to the completion at $r_{hg}$: its closed point maps there, so its local-ring homomorphism sends the maximal ideal, and every power, into the corresponding ideal of the source. In that component there is exactly one arrow with source $z$, because $s_{hg}$ is an isomorphism. Thus the composite is $a_{hg}(z)$ and its target gives $\alpha_{hg}(z)=\alpha_h(\alpha_g(z))$. The same reasoning for identity and inverse gives the identity component and the inverse indexed by $h^{-1}$. This calculation is valid on each nilpotent thickening and commutes with reduction. Associativity and the unit laws are the restrictions of those of $R\rightrightarrows T$. The completed operations therefore form a groupoid reducing to the one-object groupoid $H$.

proof.text: There is an effective map $f:\operatorname{Spec}A\to\operatorname{Spec}B\to T\to\mathcal X$, using the canonical completion homomorphism $B\to A$. Let $U_N=\operatorname{Spec}(B/\mathfrak m_B^N)$, identified with the corresponding thickening of $\operatorname{Spf}A$ by step 3. The universal arrow on $R=T\times_{\mathcal X}T$ is an isomorphism between the source and target pullbacks of the atlas object. Pull it back to $\operatorname{Spec}(B_h/\mathfrak m_h^N)$ for every $h,N$. This gives the asserted compatible isomorphisms of the two objects induced by $f$. Identity and cocycle compatibility are the identities of the universal arrow on the original groupoid, so hold after every restriction.

proof.text: Describe the formal neighbourhood on nilpotent tests: an object $\xi$ over a scheme $S$ lies in it when its restriction to a closed subscheme $S_0\subset S$, cut out by a nilpotent ideal, is locally isomorphic to the constant object $x$. This is the residual-gerbe completion convention of the statement. Choose an etale cover of $S_0$ on which such an isomorphism exists. The thickening-invariance equivalence for small etale sites lifts this cover to an etale cover of $S$; it remains covering because a nilpotent closed immersion is a homeomorphism. Refine by affine opens. On one such affine test, the isomorphism $\xi|_{S_0}\simeq x$ and $u$ give a section of $E_\xi=S\times_{\mathcal X}T$ over $S_0$. The finite diagonal makes $E_\xi$ a scheme, and the atlas definition makes $E_\xi\to S$ etale. Its flatness and unramifiedness satisfy the unique-lifting lemma. Write the affine test as $S=\operatorname{Spec}C$, with $S_0=\operatorname{Spec}(C/J)$ and $J^N=0$. Starting with the given section over $C/J$, induct on $1\leq i<N$: the closed immersion $\operatorname{Spec}(C/J^i)\subset\operatorname{Spec}(C/J^{i+1})$ is affine first order because $(J^i/J^{i+1})^2=0$. The lifting lemma gives exactly one extension of the section at each step. The final section is over $C/J^N=C$. The resulting map $S\to T$ reduces to $u$ and comes with an isomorphism to $\xi$.

proof.text: The lift in step 8 factors locally through some $U_N$. Indeed, any function vanishing at $u$ pulls back into $J$, so its $N$th power ideal pulls back to zero once $J^N=0$. Functions nonvanishing at $u$ become units: modulo $J$ they are nonzero constants, and a finite geometric series in a nilpotent element lifts their inverses. Hence the local-ring map factors through $B/\mathfrak m_B^N$, and step 3 identifies it with a map to the completed atlas. This proves local essential surjectivity onto the formal neighbourhood. For two such lifts, their isomorphisms in $\mathcal X$ are exactly the maps to $R$ by the defining 2-fibre-product equation. Modulo $J$ such a map lands in $D$, and every section of $\mathcal I_D$ pulls back into $J$. Thus it factors through the $N$th neighbourhood of $D$, which is exactly the completed arrow system of step 4. Conversely every such completed arrow is an isomorphism by step 7. This identifies the entire isomorphism sheaf, including all automorphisms.

source.place: Tag 0DR3, remark-groupoid-defo, unwinding the presentation; elementary factorization on nilpotent tests

proof.text: Stackify the completed groupoid using etale descent. Step 9 identifies its arrow sheaves with the isomorphism sheaves of the formal neighbourhood. On any covering, a cocycle of completed arrows is therefore exactly a cocycle of isomorphisms of the corresponding $\mathcal X$-objects. Effectivity of object descent in the definition of a stack glues these objects, and the sheaf condition on isomorphisms glues their maps uniquely. Step 8 and the local essential surjectivity of step 9 show that every formal-neighbourhood object is obtained this way. The functor from the stackification is consequently fully faithful and essentially surjective on every nilpotent test, naturally under pullback. Its equivalence is compatible with all reductions, since the atlas, universal arrows and lifted sections used above restrict compatibly (the latter by uniqueness). This is the asserted formal presentation together with its effective atlas object.
